thread.title: You Want To Retire Today? - Mid-America Apartment Communities Inc. (NYSE:MAA)

author: Colorado Wealth Management Fund
title: You Want To Retire Today? - Mid-America Apartment Communities Inc. (NYSE:MAA)
text:
This research report was produced by The REIT Forum with assistance from Big Dog Investments .
Rental property is one of the great ways to earn retirement income in America.
Landlords can start at a young age and begin building a successful portfolio to generate the cash flow that can replace their paycheck.
In this article, I’m going to help investors work on a landlord’s retirement plan. At The REIT Forum, our primary focus is high yields with relatively low risk. There are times, especially for trades, to invest in more risky securities. However, those tend to be exceptions.
You like real estate, but REITs are better We will look at Mid-America Apartment Communities ( MAA ). MAA is an apartment REIT with an emphasis on the non-gateway markets.
Source: MAA investor presentation
That means MAA is focused on the slightly smaller markets such as Atlanta rather than the more common gateway markets of New York and Boston. Because MAA is targeting these non-gateway markets, the properties they own trade at higher capitalization rates. That means the property produces more revenue and income for each dollar of invested capital.
Why run an apartment when MAA can do it for you?
Source: MAA investor presentation
An investor buying MAA for income is purchasing a solid dividend payer. An investor can look at the number of apartments MAA owns and the shares outstanding to figure out how many shares they would need to own to effectively own 1 rental apartment.
MAA has a solid balance sheet:
Source: MAA investor presentation
There is only moderate leverage employed in the financial structure. The investor buying MAA would effectively be acquiring the income from rental property financed mostly through equity. This structure is dramatically safer than buying real estate with a loan for 80% of the property value.
MAA trades at a significant discount to the net value of their assets.
Go with the better deal By investing in apartments through the apartment REITs, the investor is getting a much better deal than they could get by purchasing the property directly. If they wanted to buy a single condo, they would be spending significantly more money or acquiring much weaker properties. MAA also provides them with management of the apartment and all of the necessary paperwork with zero work on the shareholder side.
This is dramatically superior to what an investor would get from hiring a property manager. The only major downside investors may see is that investing through the apartment REIT requires them to have a very reasonable level of leverage. For investors who would prefer to speculate on real estate prices, it may seem preferable to have an enormous mortgage on the property.
An investor buying a rental condo and putting a mortgage on it will face a dramatically higher interest rate than MAA carries on their debts. Unlike the individual investor, MAA has a solid credit rating which enables them to acquire better interest rates on their debt.
MAA is far from the only great choice for a long-term investment in real estate. There are 6 other major apartment REITs. They are Essex Property Trust ( ESS ), Equity Residential ( EQR ), AvalonBay ( AVB ), Apartment Investment & Management Company ( AIV ), Camden Property Trust ( CPT ), UDR ( UDR ). These apartment REITs all maintain investment-grade balance sheets and all have better access to debt markets than the individual investor could ever hope to acquire on their own.
The geography behind each portfolio is different. There are a few major similarities though. With the exclusion of MAA, the largest area of emphasis is usually in California or in the other gateway markets. CPT is the other apartment REIT that has a similar avoidance of most gateway markets.
It is important for investors to recognize that the smaller REITs are using dramatically more debt leverage in their financial structures. Outside of the big 7, the leverage is much more dangerous.
I published a real-time buy alert on 5/7/2018 when the apartment REITs went on sale:
Source: YCHARTS
Investors can also look at manufactured housing parks in the same manner. There are 3 major manufactured housing park REITs. They are Equity Lifestyle ( ELS ), Sun Communities ( SUI ), UMH Properties ( UMH ). ELS and SUI use dramatically less debt than UMH. I have positions in SUI and ELS. These are strong REITs with extremely consistent growth in revenue, net operating income, FFO per share, and dividends per share. These REITs have been an excellent way for investors to accumulate wealth.
Backbone of the retirement portfolio The residential housing REITs, such as apartment REITs or manufactured housing REITs, offer an excellent foundation for building your portfolio.
Unlike many companies, they have a near certainty that their product will not become obsolete. It is possible to envision a future lacking in soft drinks or with telecommunication providers facing a technical revolution. Microsoft's ( MSFT ) dominance on operating systems could still be challenged by Google ( GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ).
A merger of Sprint ( S ) and T-Mobile ( TMUS ) could still challenge AT&T ( T ) and Verizon ( VZ ). Alternatively, changes in technology could alter the way we send data.
Remember how Netflix ( NFLX ) killed Blockbuster?
That is a clear example of the risk from major innovations.
Other reliable REITs The residential housing REITs are not limited to apartments and manufactured housing. American Homes 4 Rent ( AMH ) and Invitation Homes ( INVH ) both invest in single-family housing. The single-family housing space was previously thought to be too difficult to manage on a large scale. Most single-family rentals are owned by individual landlords. AMH and INVH are demonstrating that this process can be done more efficiently on a national scale.
Dividend yields The number 1 reason investors avoid AMH and INVH is their low dividend yields. The yields are 0.99% for AMH and 1.99% for INVH. Many investors believe they should demand a higher yield for investing in a REIT. It is true that investors should expect a return much higher than 1% to 2% when buying a REIT. These REITs cover the dividend several times over with FFO. They are reinvesting the vast majority of their earnings in acquiring additional properties. This is akin to management turning on dividend reinvestment for shareholders. In the future, I expect both REITs will raise their dividend substantially.
Rounding out the dividend portfolio There are several other dividend stocks an investor can use to build out a more diversified portfolio. These should be seen as ways to complement a portfolio built for a landlord. For instance, Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ), Pepsi ( PEP ), Coke ( KO ), Philip Morris ( PM ), Altria Group ( MO ), and Apple ( AAPL ) are all staples in many dividend portfolios. I prefer to look towards preferred shares for boosting the yield to a portfolio.
For investors interested in The REIT Forum’s preferred share ratings, see my guide to preferred shares . I also have a guide for preferred share dividend captures .
The reason I'm steering investors towards preferred equity is the certainty of the dividend, relatively stable price, and their inability to have par value or call value fluctuate.
The preferred shares dividend takes priority over the common dividend. For it to be reduced even a penny, the common dividend must be canceled entirely.
In a bankruptcy, the preferred shareholders would expect to get screwed. However, the mortgage REITs holding only agency mortgages are unlikely to ever find themselves in that situation. In an orderly liquidation of assets, those preferred shares should either get their call value or get transferred to a new company buying the husk of the mortgage REIT. Either way, they wouldn't be doing too poorly.
